paraphrase: Hearing (śravaṇa), singing (kīrtana) and reflection (manana) on Śambhu are the great means (mahāsādhana), agreeable to the Veda; reflection with the mind is the greatest; one should first hear, then practise singing and reflection.

paraphrase: Śiva alone, being Brahman, is called partless (niṣkala) and, having form, also with parts (sakala); because he is niṣkala his formless liṅga is worshipped, because he is sakala his image with form; other gods, being only sakala, are worshipped only in images, never in the formless liṅga.
speaker: Sūta (reporting Śiva's teaching as heard from his teacher)

paraphrase: Vāyu teaches the Vedic (śrauta) Pāśupata vow heard in the Atharvaśiras: on the full moon of Caitra, with the teacher's leave, one vows it for life, twelve years or a shorter term, performs the virajā fire-offering for purification of the principles, takes the ash, and - matted-haired, shaven or with one lock, naked or in ochre, bark or a single cloth - smears the limbs with the six Atharvaṇa mantras beginning 'agni', applies the three lines, and practises Śiva-yoga at the three junctures; this vow gives enjoyment and release and removes the paśu-state.
speaker: Vāyu

paraphrase: Upamanyu praises the five-syllable mantra (namaḥ śivāya), with Oṃ six syllables, as the essence of the Veda and the Śaiva scriptures, the chief means of worship and liberation, to be received from the teacher.
speaker: Upamanyu
notes: Chapter-level: titles 'pañcākṣara-māhātmya' of Vāyavīya Uttara 12 and 13 checked; content summarised from memory.

paraphrase: Śaivas on the Siddhānta path, Śaiva Pāśupatas, Śaiva Mahāvratadharas and other Śaiva Kāpālikas - keepers of Śiva's command - are to be honoured.

paraphrase: Only one whose mind is dispassionate toward seen and scriptural objects is qualified for yoga; yoga has eight limbs (yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi) or six (without yama and niyama); yama is non-harming, truth, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possession; niyama is purity, contentment, austerity, japa and devotion to the Lord (praṇidhi); posture is eightfold: svastika, padma, ardhendu, vīra, yoga, prasādhita, paryaṅka and as one likes.
speaker: Upamanyu

paraphrase: Prāṇāyāma is the restraint of the body's own breath, in three parts - exhalation, inhalation and retention - done neither fast nor slow, preceded by purification of the channels and practised gradually; its grades bring sweat and trembling, and at the highest bliss, horripilation and tears, and babbling, whirling and swooning.
speaker: Upamanyu

paraphrase: Yoga, in brief, is the unwavering activity of the mind fixed on Śiva, other activities being restrained; it is fivefold: mantra-yoga (the mind resting on the meaning of the mantra through practice of the mantra), sparśa-yoga (the same beginning with breath-control), bhāva-yoga (free of mantra and sparśa), abhāva-yoga (the universe contemplated with its parts dissolved, the real appearing as nothing) and mahā-yoga, the highest, in which Śiva's own nature alone, without adjuncts, is contemplated.
speaker: Upamanyu

paraphrase: Ten obstacles beset the practiser: sloth, severe illness, heedlessness, doubt about the place (of practice), unsteadiness of mind, lack of faith, erroneous views, suffering (of three kinds), dejection and restless craving for objects.
speaker: Upamanyu

paraphrase: When these are calmed, divine upasargas arise that indicate powers: pratibhā (knowing the subtle, hidden, past, distant and future), śravaṇa (hearing all sounds effortlessly), vārtā (knowing the speech of all beings), darśana (seeing divine forms), āsvāda (tasting divine flavours) and vedanā (divine touch); these six are powers that, when yoga is spent, become losses; seeing even a part of yoga's powers one should think liberation will likewise come.
speaker: Upamanyu

paraphrase: Through prāṇāyāma the divine states arise in order: śānti (the calming of all calamities), praśānti (the destruction of darkness within and without), dīpti (light within and without) and prasāda (the clarity of the intellect), by which all instruments inner and outer become clear.
speaker: Upamanyu

paraphrase: Meditation is at first with an object (saviṣaya) and then without (nirviṣaya); some hold there is no objectless meditation, since meditation is a continuity of cognition; the meditation with object rests on a form (like the rays of the rising sun), the objectless is awareness of the formless self; they are also called with seed and without seed; one should begin with the seeded, objective meditation and end with the seedless, objectless one.
speaker: Upamanyu
